quote: und es entsteht daher die Aufgabe sie auf das kleinste Mass zu reduciren
english: and therefore the task arises of reducing them to the smallest measure
topic: Hilbert proposes reducing a set of conditions by considering moduli of the form (φ, ψ, (x−a)^λ(y−b)^μ), then remarks that finding all integral rational functions invariant under a single integral linear substitution can be separated from binary invariant theory, and that invariance under infinitely many substitutions essentially yields only semi-invariants.

triage.modern_statement: There isn't enough here to pin down an exact question. The best guess, which is unconfirmed, is this: the modulus (φ, ψ, (x−a)^λ(y−b)^μ) suggests local membership conditions for a polynomial F in the ideal (φ, ψ) at an intersection point (a, b) of two plane curves, as in Max Noether's AF+BG 'Fundamentalsatz'. Read that way, the 'task' would be to cut the set of these local conditions down to a minimal, independent set. In modern terms that means computing the length or colength of the local quotient ring and finding a minimal set of independent linear conditions. However, the line never says which conditions are meant, so this cannot be confirmed.
triage.answered_by: No one identified. If the guess is right, the topic belongs to the late-19th-century work on Noether's fundamental theorem. C. A. Scott published a proof in Math. Ann. 52 (1899). It was later absorbed into ideal theory: Lasker's primary decomposition and Macaulay's work on inverse systems. Whether this note specifically connects to that work is not established by any source.

evidence.claim: Noether stated his Fundamental Theorem (AF+BG) in 1873. It combines a global condition with local conditions at the intersection points, which is the kind of local condition a modulus (φ, ψ, (x−a)^λ(y−b)^μ) would express.
The AF+BG theorem (Max Noether's fundamental theorem) gives local conditions for a curve's equation to lie in the ideal generated by two other curves.
C. A. Scott, 'A proof of Noether's fundamental theorem', Math. Ann. 52 (1899), is a later treatment of these conditions.
Primary decomposition in polynomial rings was first proved by Emanuel Lasker. This is the ideal-theoretic framework that took over local conditions of this kind.
